t2m.name: Air temperature (2 m)
t2m.plain: How warm the air is about head height above the ground or sea.
t2m.why: Heat-trapping gases, shrinking snow and ice, and changing cloud cover can all push surface air temperature up or down over time.

t500.name: Temperature at 500 hPa
t500.plain: How warm the air is about 5 km up, roughly halfway through the atmosphere.
t500.why: Warming at the surface can spread upward, and changes in tropical storms and heat moved by winds can make this layer warm faster or slower than the ground.

wind250.name: Wind speed at 250 hPa (jet-stream height)
wind250.plain: How fast the wind blows about 10 km up, where the jet streams run.
wind250.why: Jet streams are driven by the temperature gap between the poles and the tropics, so when that gap changes, the winds can speed up, slow down, or shift position.

tqv.name: Water vapor in the air column
tqv.plain: The total amount of invisible water vapor stacked in the air above one spot, from the ground to space.
tqv.why: Warmer air can hold more water vapor, so as temperatures change this amount tends to change too.

precip.name: Precipitation
precip.plain: How much rain and snow falls, shown as millimeters of water per day.
precip.why: Shifting wind patterns, ocean temperatures, and warmer air carrying more moisture can make some places wetter and others drier.

evap.name: Evaporation
evap.plain: How much water leaves the land and sea surface and rises into the air as vapor, in millimeters per day.
evap.why: Warmer surfaces, changing winds, and changes in plants and soil moisture can speed up or slow down evaporation.

seaice.name: Sea ice fraction
seaice.plain: The share of the ocean surface covered by floating ice, from 0 (open water) to 1 (completely covered).
seaice.why: Warmer air and ocean water melt ice faster, and open water soaks up more sunlight than ice, which can speed up further melting.

soilwet.name: Root-zone soil wetness
soilwet.plain: How wet the soil is in the top meter or so, where plant roots reach, from 0 (bone dry) to 1 (soaked).
soilwet.why: Soil wetness follows rainfall, evaporation, and snowmelt, so a change in any of them can slowly dry out or soak the ground.

snow.name: Snow mass
snow.plain: The weight of snow lying on the ground, in kilograms of water per square meter.
snow.why: Snow mass depends on how much falls in winter and how fast it melts, and both are sensitive to temperature.

runoff.name: Runoff
runoff.plain: Water that flows over or through the land toward rivers and the sea instead of soaking in, in millimeters per day.
runoff.why: Runoff rises or falls with rainfall, snowmelt, and how wet the soil already is.
